title: quantile-driven-admission-batcher: reduce starvation by adaptive queue throttles
author: Liam Chen
description:
Motivation: Continuous batching at high concurrency can lead to starvation of short/latency-sensitive requests when a small number of long contexts or large-token requests accumulate. Prior approaches used fixed timeouts or simple age-based prioritization which are brittle across workloads. This PR introduces a quantile-driven admission controller and a light-weight token-deficit tracker to adaptively throttle/serve incoming requests so that tail latencies are controlled without losing throughput.

What this change does (high level):
- Adds a QuantileAdmissionController which tracks per-route queue wait distributions and computes an adaptive admission threshold at configurable quantiles (default: 95th).
- Introduces a TokenDeficitTracker that prevents a single heavy request from repeatedly winning batch formation when it would otherwise push the observed quantile above target. The tracker reduces the effective weight of requests that recently caused quantile violations.
- Integrates admission logic into continuous batcher pipeline: admission check happens at enqueue + batch formation time to avoid building batches dominated by heavy tokens.
- Adds microbenchmarks and integration tests that simulate mixed short/long request mixes and verifies tail-latency improvement and throughput retention.
- Minor kernel interface tweak to expose estimated token footprint for pre-admission (non-breaking, small API extension).

review_comments: Amir K. (reviewer): Overall approach LGTM. Two concerns: (1) locking/contended map in QuantileAdmissionController might be a hotspot on high-shard counts, suggest using sharded counters or atomic sketches; (2) can you justify the default quantile=95? We should show sensitivity to 90/95/99 in the bench results.

Liam Chen (author): Responding: switched internal metrics to a sharded ring buffer per route to reduce contention; added a bench section showing 90/95/99 sensitivity and picked 95 as a reasonable trade-off across our canonical workloads (details in docs).

Diego M. (reviewer): TokenDeficitTracker idea is clever but please ensure it can't be gamed by adversarial request patterns (e.g., many medium requests alternating). Add a short paragraph in docs and a unit test.
Liam Chen (author): Added doc note and a fuzz-style unit test that simulates adversarial interleaving; behavior remains stable and deficit decays with configurable half-life.
ci_checks: unit-tests: fail (flaky test in batcher metrics on first run)
release_notes: Improves continuous batcher tail latency for mixed short/long workloads via a quantile-driven admission controller and deficit tracking; configurable quantile and deficit decay; non-breaking API extension to kernel token estimation.
notes_for_ops: Ops: deploy config 'quantile_batcher' feature gate off by default. When enabling, start with quantile=95 and deficit_half_life=30s and observe batcher_tail_latency.* metrics. Bench job added to CI will run on release branches to track regressions.
bench_results_summary: Local microbench: mixed 80/20 short/long token mix -> p95 latency improved ~2.1x, throughput loss <4%. Adversarial sim: no regression in p50; deficit mechanism prevented starvation over 5-minute window.
notes_from_author: This PR focuses on production-safe defaults and observability. The controller is intentionally conservative and exposes knobs to tune for extreme throughput-oriented deployments. Follow-up work: (1) explore probabilistic admission based on cost-buckets, (2) expose adaptive per-customer targets.
